Being a Parent Helps Being a Benevolent Leader: A Mixed-Method Approach

Liu, Z., Liang, Z., Wang, C., & Bian, W.

2024Journal of Business Ethics197(4), 761–784
Explore this paperOverview · Research · Citation⌄

Overview

Leadership development can draw on experiences beyond the workplace. This study examines how positive parenting experiences relate to benevolent leadership through the resources parents bring to their work roles.

Research question

How can positive parenting experiences translate into more benevolent behavior toward employees?

Methods & context

Study 1 analyzed written accounts from 13 parent-role leaders and interviews with 16 others. Study 2 used a two-wave survey of 364 leaders who were also parents in mainland China, with approximately two months between waves.

Key findings

Positive parenting experiences were linked to benevolent leadership through perspective taking. The association with perspective taking, and the indirect association with benevolent leadership, were stronger when co-parenting quality was higher.

Keywords

Benevolent leadershipParenting experiencesPerspective takingCo-parentingWork–family enrichment

Liu, Z., Liang, Z., Wang, C., & Bian, W. (2024). Being a Parent Helps Being a Benevolent Leader: A Mixed-Method Approach. Journal of Business Ethics, 197(4), 761–784. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-024-05757-1

Leadership Blossoms in Parental Warmth: Positive Parenting Practices Shape Adolescent Leader Emergence via Intrapersonal and Interpersonal Mechanisms

Liu, Z., Bian, W., & Bian, Y.

2024Journal of Youth and Adolescence53(10), 2266–2286
Explore this paperOverview · Research · Citation⌄

Overview

Leadership can begin to develop long before a formal work role. This study investigates the family as a setting for adolescent leader emergence, focusing on parental warmth and encouragement of independence.

Research question

How is parental warmth related to adolescent leader emergence, and what personal and interpersonal processes help explain this association?

Methods & context

A mixed-method design combines multi-source data from 1,255 adolescents and their parents, teachers, and peers with in-depth interviews involving 32 adolescents.

Key findings

Parental warmth was positively associated with leader emergence through two pathways: self-esteem and leader self-efficacy, and empathy and prosocial behavior. Encouragement of independence strengthened the positive association. Interviews added examples of supportive parenting practices.

Keywords

Adolescent leadershipParental warmthLeader emergenceSelf-efficacyEmpathyIndependence
Cite this paper
Liu, Z., Bian, W., & Bian, Y. (2024). Leadership Blossoms in Parental Warmth: Positive Parenting Practices Shape Adolescent Leader Emergence via Intrapersonal and Interpersonal Mechanisms. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 53(10), 2266–2286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-024-01983-y

Using Machine Learning to Explore the Predictors of Life Satisfaction Trajectories in Older Adults

Chen, H., Zhang, X., & Bian, W.*

2024Applied Psychology: Health and Well-being16(4), 2190–2203
Explore this paperOverview · Research · Citation⌄

Overview

Life satisfaction in later adulthood follows different paths over time. This study combines trajectory analysis and machine learning to identify those paths and the factors that help distinguish them.

Research question

Which trajectories of life satisfaction occur among older adults in China, and which characteristics predict membership in those trajectories?

Methods & context

Using four CHARLS waves (2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018), the study followed 2,600 adults aged 60 or older. Latent class growth and growth mixture models identified life-satisfaction trajectories; five machine-learning classifiers predicted trajectory membership.

Key findings

Four trajectories were identified. Random forest performed particularly well in predicting trajectory membership. Happiness, loneliness, body mass index, and self-rated health were important predictors; these are predictive associations rather than evidence of causal effects.

Keywords

Life satisfactionOlder adultsLongitudinal researchMachine learningTrajectory analysis
Cite this paper
Chen, H., Zhang, X., & Bian, W.* (2024). Using Machine Learning to Explore the Predictors of Life Satisfaction Trajectories in Older Adults. Applied Psychology: Health and Well-being, 16(4), 2190–2203. https://doi.org/10.1111/aphw.12579

How Does Leader Career Calling Stimulate Employee Career Growth? The Role of Career Crafting and Supervisor–Subordinate Guanxi

Ni, X., Zhu, X., Bian, W., Li, J., Pan, C., & Pan, C.

2024Leadership & Organization Development Journal45(1), 21–34
Explore this paperOverview · Research · Citation⌄

Overview

A leader’s sense of calling may matter for employees’ careers as well as the leader’s own. This study examines career crafting as a link between leader career calling and employee career growth.

Research question

How does leader career calling relate to employee career growth, and when does supervisor–subordinate guanxi strengthen this process?

Methods & context

Study 1 was a scenario experiment with 208 participants. Study 2 surveyed 490 full-time employees in a Chinese electrical-appliance enterprise in Hangzhou to test the full model of career crafting, career growth, and supervisor–subordinate guanxi.

Key findings

Career crafting mediated the relationship between leader career calling and employee career growth. Higher-quality supervisor–subordinate guanxi strengthened the calling–crafting relationship and the associated indirect relationship with career growth.

Keywords

Career callingCareer craftingCareer growthSupervisor–subordinate guanxi
Cite this paper
Ni, X., Zhu, X., Bian, W., Li, J., Pan, C., & Pan, C. (2024). How Does Leader Career Calling Stimulate Employee Career Growth? The Role of Career Crafting and Supervisor–Subordinate Guanxi. Leadership & Organization Development Journal, 45(1), 21–34. https://doi.org/10.1108/lodj-07-2023-0400

Autonomic Nervous System Response Patterns of Test-Anxious Individuals to Evaluative Stress

Bian, W., Zhang, X., & Dong, Y.

2022Frontiers in Psychology13
Explore this paperOverview · Research · Citation⌄

Overview

Evaluative situations can produce similar feelings of arousal but different physiological responses. This study examines how people with high versus low test anxiety respond to an interview-based stressor.

Research question

Do high- and low-test-anxious individuals show different autonomic and emotional responses to evaluative stress?

Methods & context

A standardized interview task induced evaluative stress in 48 participants with high test anxiety and 49 with low test anxiety. Heart-rate variability and subjective emotion were measured across baseline, stress, and recovery phases.

Key findings

Both groups reported increased arousal and showed increased low-frequency HRV. Only the high-test-anxiety group showed significant decreases in pleasantness, high-frequency HRV, and RMSSD during stress, indicating a different pattern of autonomic regulation.

Keywords

Test anxietyEvaluative stressHeart-rate variabilityAutonomic regulationEmotion
Cite this paper
Bian, W., Zhang, X., & Dong, Y. (2022). Autonomic Nervous System Response Patterns of Test-Anxious Individuals to Evaluative Stress. Frontiers in Psychology, 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.824406
